subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If Q(h,k) is the foot of the perpendicular of P(x₁,y₁) on the line ax+by+c=0 then prove that (h−x₁) : a = (k−y₁) : b = −(ax₁+by₁+c) : (a²+b²).

mark_split.label: Write h and k through r

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say what perpendicularity gives you, and what condition on Q finishes it.
formula_note: The foot Q satisfies (h−x₁)/a = (k−y₁)/b = −(ax₁+by₁+c)/(a²+b²), because Q itself lies on the line. The sibling image-of-point proof looks identical up to that last step, but there the MIDPOINT of PQ lies on the line instead of Q, and that single change is what produces the factor of 2 on the right side.

steps.memory_tip: Two slopes: the one joining P and Q, and the line's own, which reads off as −a/b.

steps.why: The foot of a perpendicular lies ON the line by definition — the drawing shows that, and it is the fact that separates this proof from the image-of-a-point proof.
common_mistakes: Drawing Q off the line, which is the image rather than the foot.
Omitting the right-angle mark, which shows that PQ is perpendicular to the line.

steps.label: Use the perpendicularity
steps.margin_note: Two marks. PQ meets the line at a right angle, so m₁m₂ = −1. Rearranged, that says (h − x₁)/a and (k − y₁)/b are EQUAL — and giving that common value the name r is what makes the rest of the proof short.
steps.memory_tip: m₁m₂ = −1 rearranges to say the two ratios are EQUAL — naming that common value r shortens everything.

lines.text: (perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1)
(multiply both sides by b/a; then cross-multiply:
a(k − y₁) = b(h − x₁), and divide both sides by ab)

recall.must_convey: That m₁m₂ = −1 gives (h − x₁)/a = (k − y₁)/b, and this common value is named r.

steps.why: Naming the common ratio r writes both h and k using ONE unknown, so a single condition on Q is enough to find it.
common_mistakes: Keeping h and k separate and ending with two unknowns and one equation.

steps.label: Write h and k through r
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Read (1) both ways round: each of h and k is now its P-coordinate plus a multiple of r. The point Q is fixed by the single number r.
steps.memory_tip: Each of h and k is its P-coordinate plus a multiple of r, so Q is fixed by one number.

lines.text: \therefore \ \dfrac{h\ - \ x_{1}}{a} = \ r\ \Rightarrow \ h\ - \ x_{1}\ = \ ar\ \Rightarrow \ h\ = \ x_{1}\ + \ ar

\dfrac{k\ - \ y_{1}}{b} = \ r\ \Rightarrow \ k\ - \ y_{1}\ = \ br\ \Rightarrow \ k\ = \ y_{1}\ + \ br

recall.must_convey: That h = x₁ + ar and k = y₁ + br.

steps.margin_note: The last three marks, and the step where this proof differs from the image proof. The FOOT of the perpendicular lies ON the line, so its coordinates satisfy the line's equation — substitute and solve for r.

steps.why: The foot of a perpendicular is by definition the point where the perpendicular MEETS the line, so it lies on the line — the second half uses that fact.
common_mistakes: Using the midpoint condition, which belongs to the image proof and gives a factor of 2.
Forgetting to take (a² + b²) common before dividing.

insider_note: The key step of the proof is naming the common ratio r, which gives h = x₁ + ar and k = y₁ + br. Q lies ON the line, so substituting those produces r directly — no distance formula is needed anywhere.
